A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same recontextualization research. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable, including the rotated response-example table. The replacement of one experimental setting does not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on evaluation gaming, incorrect coding tests, lie-detector evasion, and sycophancy, with additional results and analyses in Appendices C–F.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports new recontextualization results for evaluator-overwriting in coding and out-of-distribution sycophancy tests. Some coding comparator results are explicitly attributed to Wong et al.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix B makes the training-context denominator the default GRPO probability ratio, replacing the generation-context denominator in v1 Appendix A. This formulation was already explored as an alternative in v1 Appendix E.3. The core prompt-substitution algorithm and Expert Iteration procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The DolusChat/SOLiD deception experiment and its MASK/harmless-data regularization coverage are removed. v2 introduces Leetcode problems with an evaluator-overwriting loophole and adds user-belief matching, answer-challenge, and biased factual-answer scenarios involving TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, MMLU, and AQuA. Evaluation gaming, MBPP, and the original sycophancy/helpfulness coverage remain.

E2.justification: MBPP gains HACK→HACK inoculation-prompting comparisons in v2 Tables 11–13. The new coding comparison includes probe-, LLM-judge-, and ground-truth-based penalties and screening, alongside inoculation prompting and KL regularization. The lie-detector-specific comparison suite disappears. Inoculation comparisons already present in evaluation gaming and sycophancy are retained, not newly introduced.

E3.justification: The replacement GRPO experiment uses Qwen3-4B with thinking disabled, 200 training steps, 16 generations per question, and diversified evaluation-function names at test time. Appendix G.2 adds answer-flip, belief-matching, and bias-related accuracy protocols. The previously reported sycophancy composite evaluation reward Q−0.25S is dropped; quality and sycophancy remain separately evaluated.

E4.justification: v1's clipping/ratio-rescaling investigations, detector-strength tests, off-policy measurements, and instruction-following mitigation analyses are removed. v2 adds coding controls distinguishing generation-prompt effects from prompt contrast, irrelevant-prompt tests, and sycophancy transfer analyses. The sycophancy reward-weight, continued-recontextualization, and self-distillation ablations already existed in v1 and are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Table 17 introduces standard-deviation reporting across three seeds for the coding comparison, while its corresponding figures report standard errors. The retained five-split MBPP and three-seed sycophancy standard-error conventions are unchanged. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: New coding and out-of-distribution sycophancy results replace the SOLiD findings. For example, v2 Table 17 reports 0.3% hacking and 18.6% correctness for NEUTRAL→LOOPHOLE in the new environment, not a same-setting improvement over v1. Retained MBPP values also change: under Best-of-4 and NO HACK evaluation, the NO HACK→NO HACK hack-rate delta changes from −1.1 to +1.1 percentage points (v1 Table 14; v2 Table 12).

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A adds a common-support assumption and a formal proof that correcting the context shift by importance sampling yields the same expected gradient as standard training on the training prompt for vanilla policy gradients. v1's clipping-asymmetry and ratio-rescaling mathematical treatment is removed, and the default GRPO equations are revised.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the headline claim of preventing learned lying with preventing models from overwriting evaluation functions instead of solving coding problems. This substantially changes one principal demonstrated contribution. The overarching claim of mitigating specification gaming without correcting the supervision signal remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes regularization arising from GRPO clipping; v2 presents the uncorrected context shift as central and argues that importance correction would negate its benefits. New discussion qualifies coding success by prompt specificity and notes that sycophancy mitigation can also reduce acceptance of correct user suggestions. Lie-detector-specific mechanism explanations and instruction-following mitigation discussion disappear.

D1.justification: v2 Appendices F.2/F.7 document coding prompt templates, LoRA rank/alpha 32, learning rate 7e−5, batch size 256, and completion limits. G.7 newly specifies a 7,200-sample training mixture and four held-out test categories. Detailed DolusChat detector, reward-model, SFT, and GRPO instructions are removed. Code and synthetic-dataset access statements remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 sharpens the existing distinction from inoculation prompting. Wong et al.'s coding benchmark and Perez et al.'s behavioral evaluations are added, while deception-specific and safety-pretraining references are removed. The context-distillation relationship and the central novelty claim about contrasting generation and training prompts remain.

P1.justification: Retained exposition is condensed and edited: Sections 4.1–4.2 replace numbered setup/results subsections with inline headings, sycophancy setup details move to the appendix, and its inoculation comparison becomes a separate subsection. Discussion and limitations are rewritten, but the overall narrative structure and substantial portions of retained prose remain.

P2.justification: MBPP's main tables become a correctness-versus-hacking plot, with another plot added in the appendix. The sycophancy figure is redrawn with direct sycophancy axes, clearer KL-baseline styling, and removal of the composite-reward panel. Figure 1 and the algorithm display are redesigned, and the lie-detector figure suite is replaced by coding and transfer-evaluation displays.

improvement.justification: The new sycophancy transfer tests reduce reliance on the synthetic training distribution, while the coding comparisons strengthen evidence about prompt contrast versus inoculation and other mitigations. These provide a modest gain in empirical support. Removing SOLiD also removes distinct deception coverage and detailed mechanism and instruction-following mitigation analyses, limiting the overall improvement.
